title: Deterministic polynomial-time identity testing for general arithmetic circuits
statement: Does a uniform deterministic Turing machine decide whether a division-free arithmetic circuit over Q computes the zero polynomial in time poly(s,n,d,L), where s counts gates and wires, n counts commuting variables, L is the total binary encoding length of the rational constants, and d bounds the circuit formal degree? Require d to be bounded by a fixed polynomial in the full input encoding length. The target is polynomial bit complexity; a count of unit-cost rational operations is insufficient.
source_locator: SRC-FORMAL-007 introduction and section 5; SRC-IMPACT-011 introduction, theorems 1.1-1.2 and definitions 2.1-2.2; SRC-IMPACT-012 corollary 2.7; SRC-IMPACT-013 introduction and theorem 1. SRC-IMPACT-014 definitions 2.2.1 and 2.2.6, theorem 2.2.8 and section 2.6; SRC-IMPACT-015 section 1.1.
status_basis: The 2026 bounded-read paper identifies general deterministic PIT as open. The cited complexity references specify the formal-degree and bit-encoding conventions used here. Later restricted-model improvements were inspected; no resolution of this polynomial-formal-degree, commutative bit-complexity target was located in the scoped search.
plain_summary: A compact algebraic expression may expand into too many terms to list. Can one always decide, efficiently and without randomness, whether all terms cancel?
assumptions: The input explicitly encodes a finite directed acyclic circuit with addition and multiplication gates, commuting variables, and rational constants written as signed binary numerators and positive binary denominators. Division gates are excluded.

Let s be the number of gates plus wires, n the number of variables, and L the sum of the binary lengths of all rational-constant encodings. The complete input length N also includes graph connectivity, gate labels and variable indices.

Assign formal degree 1 to every leaf, including constant leaves; take the maximum at addition gates and the sum at multiplication gates. The promised bound d is at most a fixed polynomial in N. This is a syntactic bound, not merely the degree of the final polynomial after cancellation.
Running time means deterministic Turing-machine bit operations, including exact-number handling and construction of any evaluation points. Huge integers are not unit-cost objects.
White-box access exposes the encoded circuit. A black-box extension must separately specify its evaluation interface, size and degree bounds, query encodings and all bit costs.
The target is uniform and unconditional, with no randomness, nonuniform advice or unproved hardness assumption.
scope: Commutative arithmetic circuits over Q of polynomially bounded formal degree, in the binary Turing model. No depth, read-count or multilinearity restriction is imposed. The unbounded-formal-degree problem and black-box interfaces are separate variants.
target: An unconditional deterministic identity test with polynomial bit complexity for the stated inputs, or a clearly identified partial result for a literature-supported restricted circuit class.
success_criteria: Give a complete algorithm and prove correctness for every permitted input, including zero and constant circuits.
Prove uniform construction and a polynomial bit-time bound, including every subroutine and exact-number operation; do not hide an identity-testing oracle or exponential-length evaluation point.
If a restriction is imposed, identify it in the theorem and compare it against current results for exactly that class.
known_results: Random evaluation supplies a one-sided-error identity test; derandomization and explicit hitting sets remain central goals (SRC-FORMAL-007).

Kaplan and Shpilka give polynomial-time white-box and quasipolynomial-time black-box PIT for non-multilinear read-four formulas, in characteristic zero or at least five. A read counts a variable occurrence at a leaf, not its final degree. No constant-depth assumption is imposed (SRC-IMPACT-011).

Guo's September 2026 note removes squarefreeness for depth-four circuits with at most three product summands and constant bottom degree, in the stated algebraic model over arbitrary fields (SRC-IMPACT-012).
Černý and Seppelt give logspace interreductions between PIT, multiplicity tree automata equivalence and a specified bounded-treewidth graph problem (SRC-IMPACT-013).

A large-integer Kronecker substitution reduces rational PIT to exact circuit evaluation; its compact arithmetic description does not make its binary evaluation inexpensive (SRC-IMPACT-014, theorem 2.6.3).
prerequisites: Arithmetic circuits, formal degree, rational encodings and Turing-machine bit complexity

significance: PIT is a central derandomization problem linked to circuit lower bounds. Its reductions also connect algebraic identity testing with automata equivalence and graph algorithms; a restricted result needs its own significance assessment.

relations.explanation: Both concern removing randomness. The general BPP question is broader; this entry fixes an algebraic decision problem.
PIT and arithmetic circuit lower bounds are linked by hardness-versus-randomness results; no unconditional equivalence between these two entries is asserted.

methods: Source-based structural analysis of restricted circuits
Exact symbolic examples and algorithm verification
obstacles: Cancellations can conceal a nonzero polynomial from an inadequate evaluation set.
A reduction can increase size, degree, depth or read count beyond the permitted class.
A short arithmetic algorithm can have unaccounted bit complexity or require a hidden randomized subroutine.

steps: Match the field, rational encoding, formal-degree convention, circuit representation, access model and uniform bit-time requirement against the exact theorem.
Audit every reduction and subroutine for correctness and bit complexity; include query lengths, intermediate-number sizes and preservation of the promised formal degree.
Use independently constructed exact instances to detect defects, while retaining the universal proof obligation.
For a hitting set, prove both deterministic construction and that every nonzero member of the class is hit; a list that works on a benchmark is insufficient.
validation.human_review_difficulty: Specialist review is required for the structural argument and the uniform complexity bound.
validation.statement_alignment: Known restricted-model algorithms, randomized tests, finite benchmark agreement, unit-cost huge-integer evaluations and noncommutative matrix substitutions do not by themselves meet this bit-complexity target.
